title: An export tax would raise public revenue that a reservation scheme forgoes
oneLiner: Reservation moves gas; a tax also moves money.
body: A levy on exports accrues to the budget; a reservation obligation does not. Senator Pocock's dissent paired a 25 per cent export tax with a cap on decommissioning-cost deductions as a revenue package. A cross-party Senate committee agreed the government should revisit gas taxation once the Middle East conflict ends, without reaching consensus on the design.
contextBackground: The revenue argument is the part of the tax case that does not depend on the price effect at all.
contextDisagreement: Agreed in principle. Opponents say the revenue comes at the cost of investment in new supply, which is the same objection made to reservation.

evidenceItems.citation: ABC News, 7 May 2026 — Pocock dissenting report and Senate committee on gas taxation

otherClaim.title: Australia should tax gas exports rather than reserve gas for domestic buyers

claimItself.title: Australia should tax gas exports rather than reserve gas for domestic buyers
claimItself.oneLiner: The competing proposal from the Greens and Senator Pocock: price the exports, do not ration them.
claimItself.body: Instead of requiring producers to set gas aside, an export levy would make overseas sales less attractive relative to domestic ones and return revenue to the public. The Greens argued the reservation policy was written by the industry for the industry; Senator David Pocock's dissenting report to a Senate committee recommended a 25 per cent tax on all gas exports. The government ruled out gas tax increases in the May 2026 budget, citing fuel security during the Middle East conflict.
